traveler: Richard I of England, Cœur de Lion
title: Oxford to Châlus: the Crusade, the Captivity, and the Song
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Oxford, Beaumont Palace
stops.campa: On the eighth of September, in the King's own house at Beaumont outside the north gate of Oxford, Eleanor of Aquitaine bears her third son to Henry II of England. They name him Richard. He is not born to the English crown — two elder brothers stand before him, William already dead in infancy, Henry the Young King living — but he is born to Aquitaine, his mother's inheritance, and to the restless troubadour blood of her grandfather Duke William IX, first poet of the Provençal tongue. The bells of Oxford ring for a Plantagenet, not yet knowing which one.
suggested_refs: The site of Beaumont Palace, Oxford, marked near Beaumont Street, where Richard and his brother John were both born
sources: Gillingham, Richard I (Yale, 1999)
Flori, Richard the Lionheart: King and Knight

stops.name: Poitiers, the court of Eleanor
stops.campa: Eleanor withdraws to Poitiers and gathers about her the poets of the Aquitainian tongue: Bernart de Ventadorn sings for her there, and the young Richard grows up inside the sound of the langue d'oc rather than the Anglo-Norman French of his father's court. He learns to make verses as other princes learn to hawk. In later years two of his own songs survive, a tenson traded with the Dauphin d'Alvernha and, from prison, a plainer song of his own grief, but the ear for it, and the grief it will one day carry, are shaped here, at his mother's knee.
suggested_refs: Bernart de Ventadorn's chansons, composed for Eleanor's court at Poitiers
sources: Gillingham, Richard I
Bull, Eleanor of Aquitaine: Lord and Lady

stops.name: Poitiers and Limoges, the investiture as Duke of Aquitaine
stops.campa: At Poitiers, in the abbey church of Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand, the archbishop of Bordeaux and the bishop of Poitiers set the lance and banner of the duchy into Richard's hands: he is fourteen years old. Days later he enters Limoges in solemn procession and is given the ring of Saint Valerie, virgin martyr and patroness of Aquitaine, drawn from her own reliquary, mantle, coronet, sword, spurs, all laid on him in the old formula kept at Saint-Étienne. Aquitaine, which answers to no duke gladly, is told it now has one: Eleanor's son, crowned in his mother's country before he is crowned anywhere else.
suggested_refs: The reliquary ring of Saint Valerie of Limoges, given in the ducal investiture
sources: Gillingham, Richard I
the twelfth-century Limoges ordo of ducal investiture (Saint-Étienne)

stops.name: Taillebourg, the impregnable castle taken in three days
stops.campa: The barons of Poitou rise again, and Geoffroi de Rancon shuts himself inside Taillebourg, a rock fortress on the Charente held, the country says, by no power but God's, cliff on three sides, triple wall on the fourth. Richard does not storm it. He burns the fields and vineyards around it for a week, cuts off every road, until the garrison, starving, sallies out to break the siege and is routed in the open; Richard rides in through their own open gates on their heels. The impregnable castle falls in three days. No baron of the south doubts him again.
suggested_refs: The ruined keep of Taillebourg above the Charente
sources: Gillingham, Richard I
Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Henrici Secundi

stops.name: Martel, the death of the Young King
stops.campa: Henry the Young King, crowned in his father's lifetime and never given power to match the crown, dies of a bloody flux at Martel in the Limousin, still in arms against both father and brother. On his deathbed he sends for a hairshirt and a rope, has himself laid on ashes with a stone for a pillow, and begs his father's forgiveness, which reaches him too late, by letter alone. Richard, his rival and heir in one, is now Henry II's eldest living son and undisputed heir to England, Normandy, Anjou, and his own Aquitaine besides, an inheritance bought with a brother's unquiet death.
suggested_refs: The tomb tradition of Henry the Young King, buried at Rouen Cathedral
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Henrici Secundi
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Tours, the taking of the cross
stops.campa: Word reaches Tours of the disaster at Hattin: Saladin has broken the army of Jerusalem, taken the True Cross, and by autumn the Holy City itself. Before his own father has so much as agreed to go, Richard — Count of Poitou, not yet king — kneels and takes the cross from the archbishop's hand, the first prince north of the Alps to do so. It is an act aimed as much at Henry II as at Saladin: the son moves before the father dares. He will spend two more years fighting Henry for the throne before he spends a single day fighting for Jerusalem.
suggested_refs: The cathedral of Saint-Gatien, Tours, on the traditional site of Richard's crusading vow
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Henrici Secundi
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Chinon, the death of Henry II
stops.campa: Two days after his army breaks Henry's at Ballans, Richard learns his father is dying at Chinon. He rides to him and finds the old king already past speech, wasted by fever and by the discovery, the chroniclers say it broke him past the wound of any battle, that his youngest son John, his last hope, had also gone over to the rebels. Henry dies on the sixth of July. Richard kneels by the bier; the chroniclers report the corpse's nose bleeds afresh at his approach, an old ordeal-sign of a murderer's presence, and men whisper of it, though the Church absolves him.
suggested_refs: The chapel of Chinon, traditional site of Henry II's deathbed
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Henrici Secundi
Gerald of Wales, De Principis Instructione

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the coronation
stops.campa: Richard is anointed and crowned in Westminster Abbey with the ancient rite: the oil on his breast, head, and hands, the mantle, the sword of justice, the crown set on him by the Archbishop of Canterbury. He has ordered that no Jew or woman cross the threshold of the feast that follows, a precaution too weak: that same evening a mob turns on the Jewish delegation come to bring gifts, and the massacre spreads by morning through the city and, in the weeks after, to York. Richard, furious, hangs some of the ringleaders; the crown he has just received is already stained with blood not his own.
suggested_refs: Westminster Abbey's coronation rite, essentially unchanged since Richard's crowning
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Vézelay, the meeting of the two kings
stops.campa: Beneath the great Romanesque tympanum of the Madeleine at Vézelay, where the Second Crusade was also preached, Richard and Philip Augustus of France meet with their combined armies and, on the fourth of July, set out together southward: two kings who trust each other only as far as the road requires, bound by oath not to attack each other's lands while the other is on crusade. Pilgrims and soldiers of a dozen tongues fill the hillside town. It is the largest army either king has commanded, and the last time the two of them will travel as allies rather than enemies.
suggested_refs: The tympanum of the basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine, Vézelay
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Marseille, awaiting the fleet
stops.campa: Richard reaches Marseille ahead of his own fleet, still beating down from England around Iberia, and will not wait: impatient by nature, he hires ships on the spot and sails on toward Sicily, working down the Italian coast — Genoa, Portofino, Pisa, Naples — visiting shrines and towns as a tourist-king might, while his official navy trails weeks behind him under its Dieppe captains. It is a pattern that will recur throughout the crusade: the plan made in council, and then Richard, unable to sit still inside it, moving faster than anyone expected him to move.
suggested_refs: The Vieux-Port of Marseille, from which the crusading fleets departed
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Messina, the taking of the Griffon city
stops.campa: Messina, a Greek and Lombard town the crusaders call Griffon-land, quarrels with the newcomers over prices and lodging; Tancred of Lecce, the usurping King of Sicily, has also imprisoned Richard's widowed sister Joan, dowager queen, and withholds her dower. When a riot kills some of his men, Richard does not negotiate: at dawn on the fourth of October he storms the city, plants his standard on its walls before Philip's men have armed, and holds it as surety until Tancred releases Joan and pays a settlement in gold. Messina falls to a crusader king before a single blow is struck against the infidel.
suggested_refs: Richard's golden standard, raised over Messina's citadel on 4 October 1190
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi

stops.name: Messina, the abbot Joachim and the Antichrist
stops.campa: Wintering at Messina, Richard sends for Joachim of Fiore, the Calabrian abbot famous through Christendom for reading the Apocalypse of John as a map of ages still to come. Before the assembled court he asks the old man plainly when the Antichrist will be born and where. Joachim answers that he is born already, in the city of Rome, and will rise to the papal chair itself before the end. The court is troubled; Richard, setting out to fight one kind of enemy in the East, receives instead a prophecy pointed at the heart of Christendom, and rides on toward Jerusalem no less uneasy for it.
suggested_refs: The writings of Joachim of Fiore on the Apocalypse, discussed before Richard's court at Messina
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Reeves, The Influence of Prophecy in the Later Middle Ages

stops.name: Messina, departure and the storm
stops.campa: On the tenth of April the great fleet, some two hundred ships by the chroniclers' count, puts out from Messina for Cyprus and the Holy Land. A violent storm strikes within days and scatters it across the sea: several vessels are lost outright, and three, including the great ship carrying Richard's bride-to-be, Berengaria of Navarre, and his sister Joan, are driven onto the coast of Cyprus, out of the King's sight and, for some anxious days, out of his knowledge whether they still live.
suggested_refs: The scattered route of the fleet, April 1191, as recorded in Ambroise's Estoire
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Itinerarium Peregrinorum

stops.name: Limassol, the wrecked ships and the tyrant's insult
stops.campa: Isaac Komnenos, the Greek adventurer who has made himself self-styled emperor of Cyprus, plunders the wrecked crews washed onto his shore and refuses the ship carrying Berengaria and Joan leave to take on water, hoping to ransom or seize the women himself. Richard arrives on the sixth of May, hears it, and does not wait for council: he lands his knights through the surf under fire, scatters Isaac's troops on the beach, and takes Limassol before nightfall. Within days the whole conquest of the island — undertaken almost as an afterthought, to punish an insult to two women — is under way.
suggested_refs: The medieval castle of Limassol, site of Richard's landing
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Itinerarium Peregrinorum

stops.name: Limassol, the marriage to Berengaria of Navarre
stops.campa: In the small chapel of Saint George within Limassol castle, Richard marries Berengaria of Navarre, whom Eleanor herself had brought south from Spain to meet him at Messina the winter before. The Bishop of Évreux says the mass; Berengaria is crowned Queen of England in the same rite, the only English queen ever crowned outside England. It is a marriage of alliance, made between two campaigns, on conquered ground, with the smoke of the island's subjugation still rising a few miles off, and it will remain, to the end of Richard's life, more a treaty kept than a love matched.
suggested_refs: The Chapel of Saint George in Limassol Castle, site of the wedding and coronation
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Itinerarium Peregrinorum
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Cape Apostolos Andreas, the submission and the silver chains
stops.campa: Isaac's field army breaks near Tremithousa; he runs to the mountain castle of Kantara, and from there down the long horn of the Karpass to the island's last headland, Cape Apostolos Andreas, where the sea ends the road. He surrenders on one condition: that he, an emperor by his own naming, not be bound in iron like a common man. Richard, with the courtesy he can afford a beaten enemy, grants it, and has silver chains made specially to fetter him. Cyprus, taken almost by accident in three weeks, becomes the crusaders' forward base and a Latin kingdom outlasting every mainland conquest of the crusade by three hundred years.
suggested_refs: The monastery and headland of Apostolos Andreas at the tip of the Karpass, where Isaac Komnenos surrendered
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Edbury, The Kingdom of Cyprus and the Crusades

segments.name: The Siege and Fall of Acre

stops.name: Acre, the renewed siege
stops.campa: Richard reaches Acre on the eighth of June, two years into a siege that has itself become a small trapped city, Christian besiegers ringed by Saladin's relieving army, both camps starving under the same sky. Philip Augustus arrived weeks earlier and has made little headway; Richard's engineers and his siege engines, among them a catapult he names Bad Neighbour, change the mathematics of the wall within days. He falls ill soon after landing, with a wasting fever the army calls arnaldia, and directs the siege from a stretcher, having himself carried to the front to loose crossbow bolts at the defenders from his sickbed.
suggested_refs: The medieval walls of Acre, breached by the siege engines of 1191
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad, The Rare and Excellent History of Saladin

stops.name: Acre, the city falls
stops.campa: On the twelfth of July, after weeks of mining and battery, the garrison of Acre — cut off, its walls broken, no relief able to reach it through the crusader lines — surrenders on terms: the city, its Christian captives, the True Cross taken at Hattin, two hundred thousand gold dinars, and the release of some sixteen hundred named prisoners, all within a month. The banners of England, France, and, over Conrad of Montferrat's objection, of Leopold of Austria, are raised on the walls together. Two years of siege end in an afternoon; the two kings enter the city they have spent their armies to take.
suggested_refs: Baha ad-Din's eyewitness account of the fall of Acre, 12 July 1191
sources: Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad
Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte

stops.name: Acre, the Duke's banner cast down
stops.campa: Duke Leopold V of Austria, kinsman of the Emperor and the senior surviving prince of the German contingent since Barbarossa's death on the road, sets his own banner beside the royal standards on the walls, claiming a share of a conquest his small force scarcely earned. Richard's men, by some accounts on Richard's own order, tear it down and throw it in the ditch with the filth of the siege camp. It is a small insult, quickly given and quickly forgotten by the man who gave it. Leopold does not forget it, and eighteen months from now the debt will fall due outside Vienna.
suggested_refs: The red-white-red arms of Austria, said to originate in Leopold's blood-soaked surcoat at Acre
sources: Itinerarium Peregrinorum
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Ayyadieh, the massacre of the hostages
stops.campa: The deadline for Saladin's ransom passes unmet — the gold short, the Cross not produced, the prisoners not yet freed on his side — and Richard, reading it as bad faith rather than the genuine difficulty it may also be, orders some twenty-seven hundred Muslim captives of Acre led onto the plain of Ayyadieh in full sight of Saladin's watching army and put to the sword. His own chroniclers call it just retaliation for Christian dead; the Arabic sources call it what it plainly also is. Saladin, in answer, kills the Christian prisoners still in his hands. Neither side offers terms again for a long while.
suggested_refs: Baha ad-Din's eyewitness account of the massacre, watched from the Muslim camp
sources: Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad
Geoffrey de Vinsauf, Itinerarium Peregrinorum

segments.name: The March to Jerusalem, and the Boy Knight of Acre

stops.name: Arsuf, the battle in the pines
stops.campa: Marching south along the coast toward Jaffa, shadowed the whole way by Saladin's harrying cavalry, Richard holds his column in tight order through the forest of Arsuf until the Hospitallers at the rear, stung past bearing, break formation and charge without orders. Richard, rather than let the charge be wasted, commits the whole army behind it in a single controlled shock Saladin's line cannot absorb. It is the first open field battle Saladin has lost to a Christian king. Richard, the chroniclers say, is seen everywhere in the melee, unhorsed once, fighting to remount surrounded, Cœur de Lion earning, in one afternoon, the name that outlives him.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Arsuf, at Tel Arsuf on the coast north of Jaffa
sources: Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad
Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte

stops.name: Jaffa, the port refortified
stops.campa: The army reaches the ruins of Jaffa, razed years before, and Richard sets it building again as the crusaders' forward base and supply port, the hinge between the coast and any march inland toward Jerusalem. He works alongside the masons himself, the chroniclers note, in defiance of royal custom. From here he opens correspondence with al-Adil, Saladin's brother, trading gifts and, eventually, a half-serious proposal that his widowed sister Joan marry al-Adil and the two of them hold a joint kingdom over Jerusalem, a peace by marriage-bed that founders, in the end, on Joan's own fury at being offered as its price.
suggested_refs: The rebuilt walls of Jaffa, crusader base for the march inland
sources: Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad
Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte

stops.name: Beit Nuba, the first turning back
stops.campa: By the first days of January the army has fought and marched its way to Beit Nuba, a bare dozen miles from Jerusalem's walls, close enough that scouts ride out and report the very look of the city gates. Then the winter breaks in earnest — cold rain, hail, roads turned to mud that stalls the supply carts — and the council of barons, weighing a siege they cannot supply against a relieving army they cannot yet see, votes to fall back to the coast rather than risk being trapped before walls they might not carry. Richard, who wanted the city as much as any man in the host, gives the order to retreat.
suggested_refs: Ambroise's account of the retreat from Beit Nuba, January 1192
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Itinerarium Peregrinorum

stops.name: Acre, the knighting of the boy al-Kamil
stops.campa: In a lull of the war's diplomacy, al-Adil brings his young son to Richard's camp at Acre, a boy of eleven or twelve, already called al-Kamil, "the Perfect," within his own house. Richard, who has made a courteous friend of the father across a dozen truces and embassies, receives the son with open pleasure, dresses him, and dubs him knight with his own hand in the fashion of the Franks: the accolade, the belt, the spurs. It is a small ceremony between enemies who like each other better than their wars allow them to say, and the boy carries the memory of it into the sultanate he will one day rule.
suggested_refs: The later reign of al-Kamil as Sultan of Egypt, who would receive Francis of Assisi unarmed in his own camp in 1219
sources: Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad (tradition)
secondary accounts of Ayyubid-Angevin diplomacy at Acre, spring 1192

stops.name: Beit Nuba, the shield before Jerusalem
stops.campa: A second advance brings the army back to Beit Nuba in June, and this time the French and English captains fall out openly: Hugh of Burgundy and the French will have a siege of Jerusalem outright; Richard argues, against his own evident wish, that the army lacks strength to hold what it might take, and that Egypt, not Jerusalem, is the sultan's real spine to break. Riding out on patrol, he comes to a hilltop from which the city itself is visible for the first time, and, the legend tells, will not look: he raises his shield before his eyes, saying he is not worthy to see the city he cannot deliver.
suggested_refs: The hill traditionally identified as Nebi Samwil / Montjoie, from which crusaders first sighted Jerusalem
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
later medieval tradition of the shield before Jerusalem

stops.name: Jaffa, the battle and the King's last charge
stops.campa: Saladin strikes at Jaffa while Richard is still at Acre, and the town falls before Richard's galleys can beat down the coast; landing at speed with a handful of knights, Richard wades ashore through the surf, drives the garrison of Saladin's men still looting the town back out through the gates, and holds the ruined walls with barely enough men to be called a garrison. Days later Saladin's whole army tries again in the open field before the town; Richard, on a borrowed horse, charges the Muslim line so far ahead of his own knights that Saladin himself, watching, sends him a fresh mount rather than see so brave a man unhorsed and killed by chance.
suggested_refs: Baha ad-Din's account of Saladin sending Richard two horses during the battle of Jaffa
sources: Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad
Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte

stops.name: Jaffa, the treaty and the pilgrims allowed
stops.campa: Both sides are spent. On the second of September Richard and Saladin conclude, through al-Adil, the Treaty of Jaffa: a three-year truce, Jerusalem to remain in Muslim hands but open to unarmed Christian pilgrims, a strip of coast from Tyre to Jaffa left to the Franks. Richard himself, ill again and unwilling to enter the city he cannot hold as a conqueror, does not make the pilgrimage; his soldiers go up to the Holy Sepulchre in parties under safe-conduct while their king remains on the coast. He is remembered as swearing he would return and finish what this crusade left undone. He never does.
stops.quote: If the land were to be lost in his time, he would rather have it taken into Richard's mighty power than see it go into the hands of any other prince he had ever seen.
stops.quote_source: Saladin's reply to Richard's truce embassy, Itinerarium Peregrinorum et Gesta Regis Ricardi, reported under late July 1192, in the negotiations that ended in the Treaty of Jaffa
suggested_refs: The text of the Treaty of Jaffa, 2 September 1192
sources: Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad
Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Itinerarium Peregrinorum

stops.name: Acre, the departure
stops.campa: On the ninth of October Richard sails from Acre for home, word having reached him that Philip Augustus is conspiring with his brother John against the Angevin lands he has left ungoverned for three years. He leaves the crusade's work half finished and its army dispersed to a dozen quarrels over who will rule what remains of the kingdom of Jerusalem. The chroniclers give him a last look back at the coastline: he is said to pray, as the sails fill, that God grant him to return one day and see the Holy City again. Instead it is the last time in his life he sees the Levant.
suggested_refs: Ambroise's farewell account of the departure from Acre, October 1192
sources: Ambroise, L'Estoire de la Guerre Sainte
Itinerarium Peregrinorum

stops.name: Corfu, the pirate galleys
stops.campa: The fleet, wary of the ports of southern Italy and Sicily where Richard has enemies, works its way up the Adriatic; off Corfu, on the eleventh of November, Richard's ship falls in with a pair of pirate galleys. Rather than fight or flee them he hires them outright. They are the fastest, most anonymous vessels he can find, for a passage he already knows must be made quietly, by a route no one expects a crusading king to take. He travels now with only a handful of companions, his own fleet sent ahead or scattered: a king trying to vanish into the sea he has just conquered a kingdom's worth of enemies upon.
suggested_refs: The Corfu roadstead, last safe harbor before the Adriatic crossing
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Aquileia, the wreck and the landfall
stops.campa: A storm in the small hours of the second and third of December drives the hired galleys onto the coast near Aquileia, at the head of the Adriatic, deep inside territory hostile to him on every side, ringed by lords loyal to the Emperor Henry VI or to the kin of his own crusade-enemy Conrad of Montferrat. Richard comes ashore with a handful of men, disguises himself as a merchant pilgrim, some say as a Knight Templar, and resolves to strike overland through the mountains for his brother-in-law's lands in Saxony rather than risk the open roads of Italy, where his own name is a death warrant.
suggested_refs: The Roman ruins of Aquileia, traditional site of Richard's landfall
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Ralph of Coggeshall, Chronicon Anglicanum

stops.name: Friesach, the ride in disguise
stops.campa: For nineteen days Richard rides north and east through Carinthia and lower Austria with only William de l'Étang and a German-speaking boy for company, posing as a merchant returning from pilgrimage, paying too freely for a poor man and giving himself away by wearing, under his rough cloak, a jewelled ring he cannot bring himself to sell. At the hardest stretch they cover some hundred and fifty miles in three days, sleeping little, eating worse, twice nearly taken at inns where local lords grow suspicious of a traveller who will not give his name and pays in gold no merchant carries.
suggested_refs: The overland route traditionally traced from Friuli through Carinthia toward Vienna
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Vienna, Erdberg, the capture
stops.campa: Fifty miles short of the Moravian border and safety, sick with fever and unable to ride further, Richard stops to rest at an inn in Erdberg, a suburb of Vienna, sending the boy into the market for provisions and, fatally, to change money too freely for a servant's purse. The boy is stopped, questioned, and under pressure names his master; Leopold of Austria's men surround the inn. Richard is found in the kitchen, it is said, turning a spit, and refuses to yield his sword to any but the Duke himself. Leopold comes in person: the man whose banner was thrown in the ditch at Acre now holds the King of England prisoner.
suggested_refs: The traditional site of the inn at Erdberg where Richard was taken, 21 December 1192
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Ralph of Coggeshall, Chronicon Anglicanum

stops.name: Dürnstein, the castle on the Danube
stops.campa: Leopold holds his prize secretly at first, then openly, in the castle of Dürnstein above a bend of the Danube, guarded by the castellan Hadmar von Kuenring. News of an English king vanished on the road home spreads through Europe faster than any confirmed report of where he is; a later and much-loved legend fills the gap with the minstrel Blondel de Nesle, wandering castle to castle singing the first half of a song only he and Richard know, until from behind Dürnstein's wall a voice takes up the second verse. In truth the Emperor has already written to announce the capture. The legend outlives the correction.
suggested_refs: The ruined keep of Dürnstein Castle above the Danube, and the Blondel legend it carries
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
the Minstrel of Reims (13th c.), first written source for the Blondel legend

stops.name: Speyer, brought before the Emperor
stops.campa: Leopold surrenders his prisoner to the Emperor Henry VI, who nurses larger grievances against Richard, old quarrels over Sicily and Tancred, and Richard's friendship with Henry's rival for that crown. Brought before the imperial Diet at Speyer, formally accused of conspiring against the Emperor's cousin and of the murder of Conrad of Montferrat, Richard defends himself alone, without counsel, in a speech the chroniclers say moves hardened enemies to tears, regal, unbroken, as though he sat on his own throne at Lincoln or Caen. He is not acquitted, but the mood of the hall turns, and the Emperor shifts from trial toward the arithmetic of ransom.
suggested_refs: Speyer Cathedral, imperial seat where Richard's trial and defense took place
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
William the Breton, Philippide

stops.name: Trifels, the fortress and the prison song
stops.campa: Moved to Trifels castle in the Rhineland hills, held under harsher watch than Dürnstein's, Richard composes — in French and in the langue d'oc together, the two tongues of his mother's court — a song addressed to his half-sister Marie of Champagne: Ja nus hons pris ne dira sa raison, no man who is imprisoned can tell his case aright, save sorrowfully. He complains not of chains but of a slower cruelty: two winters gone and no lord or kinsman come to ransom him, while lesser men are freed for less. It is the truest surviving record of his own voice, spoken in the one tongue captivity cannot take from a poet's son.
stops.quote: Ja nus hons pris ne dira sa raison / Adroitement, se dolantement non; / Mais par confort puet il faire chançon. / Assez ai d'amis, mais povre sont li don; / Honte i avront, se por ma reançon / Sui ça deux yvers pris.
stops.quote_source: "Ja nus hons pris" (RS 1891), composed by Richard I in captivity, 1193 — text normalized from the chansonnier tradition; the place is given variously as Dürnstein or Trifels
suggested_refs: The sole surviving melody and text of Ja nus hons pris, preserved in the chansonnier manuscripts
sources: Ja nus hons pris, Richard I (RS 1891)
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Worms, the ransom set
stops.campa: The Emperor and his council set the price of the King of England's freedom at one hundred and fifty thousand marks of silver, some three times the annual revenue of the whole English crown, to be paid before Richard is released, with hostages of high rank held against the balance. Word crosses to England within weeks. Eleanor of Aquitaine, seventy years old and regent again in her son's absence as she was once in her husband's, begins stripping the kingdom for it: a quarter of every man's income and goods, the gold and silver plate of the churches, scutage on every knight's fee, wool sold off the sheep's back before shearing.
suggested_refs: Worms Cathedral, where the ransom terms were formally set
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Mainz, the ransom paid, the release
stops.campa: Eleanor herself, not trusting the business to any deputy, crosses to Germany with the ransom in the depths of winter to see her favorite son delivered with her own eyes. At Mainz on the fourth of February the sum is paid, the hostages exchanged, and Richard, in a final humiliation the Emperor extracts at the last hour, is made to kneel and surrender England itself as a fief held from the Empire, receiving it back at once as vassal, a homage the English council will simply refuse to honor afterward. Then, at last, mother and son ride west together, free, toward the sea and home.
suggested_refs: Mainz Cathedral, site of the formal release and the surrender-and-refeoffment of the English crown
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Gillingham, Richard I

segments.name: The Return and the Last Years

stops.name: Sandwich, the landing
stops.campa: Richard lands at Sandwich in Kent on the thirteenth of March, more than four years after he first sailed for the Holy Land, king of a country he has now spent barely six months of his reign actually inhabiting. Church bells ring the length of the Kentish coast; he goes first, on foot, to give thanks at the shrine of Thomas Becket in Canterbury before anything else, the murdered archbishop his father's great sin, the pilgrimage a son's atonement offered on his own behalf as much as his father's. Then he turns toward London, toward the throne, and toward a brother who thought him dead or fixed for good in a German cell.
suggested_refs: The port of Sandwich, Richard's landing place, 13 March 1194
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Ralph of Coggeshall, Chronicon Anglicanum

stops.name: Winchester, the second coronation
stops.campa: To wash out the stain of captivity — a king who has knelt to an emperor must be seen, publicly, wearing his crown as a free man again — Richard holds a second, ceremonial crown-wearing at Winchester Cathedral on the seventeenth of April, the old West Saxon capital, robed and crowned anew before the assembled magnates of England. It is not a fresh coronation in the sacramental sense, no new anointing, but theater as carefully staged as any of his sieges: the message, to England and to Philip of France alike, is that the Lionheart is home, unbroken, and already turning to the war he has been cheated of for five years running.
suggested_refs: Winchester Cathedral, site of the 1194 crown-wearing
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Fréteval, the rout of the French king
stops.campa: Within weeks Richard is in Normandy making war on Philip Augustus, who spent the captivity years carving into Angevin lands on the promise Richard would never return. At Fréteval, near Vendôme, Richard catches the French army in retreat and routs it outright; Philip flees the field so fast he abandons his entire baggage train, including his personal seal and the royal archives, charters, tax rolls, the names of every spy and agent Philip keeps inside Richard's own duchies. It is as much an intelligence coup as a battle, and hands Richard, for the first time since the crusade, the clear upper hand over the king who once called himself his brother-in-arms.
suggested_refs: The captured archive of Philip Augustus, seized at Fréteval and later deposited in the Tower of London
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
William the Breton, Philippide

stops.name: Les Andelys, Château Gaillard, the year-old daughter
stops.campa: On a chalk spur above the Seine at Les Andelys, in defiance of a treaty forbidding him to fortify the spot, Richard raises in a single year the castle he calls his masterpiece: triple-walled, machicolated, its keep faced with pointed buttresses no siege engine of the age can find purchase against. Riding out to see it nearing completion, he is said to look up at the pale new stone and call it, in delight, how fair is this year-old daughter of mine, Château Gaillard, the saucy, the insolent castle. He boasts he could hold it were its walls made of butter. Philip Augustus will take it after Richard's death, but never in his lifetime.
stops.quote: Behold, how fair is this year-old daughter of mine!
stops.quote_source: Richard on Château Gaillard, c. 1197-98 — the saying is carried by the Anglo-Norman chronicle tradition; the wording here is the received English rendering, and no single chronicle text could be fixed as its origin
suggested_refs: The ruins of Château Gaillard, above Les Andelys on the Seine
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Gillingham, Richard I

stops.name: Châlus-Chabrol, the crossbow bolt and the forgiveness
stops.campa: Besieging the minor castle of Châlus-Chabrol over a disputed treasure of Roman gold, which Richard claims by his overlord's right, he rides too close to the walls unarmored in the evening light, and a crossbow bolt fired by a defender, a boy some chroniclers name Bertrand de Gourdon, strikes him in the shoulder. A clumsy surgeon's cutting turns the wound gangrenous within days. Brought the boy who shot him, and told he had lost a father and two brothers to Richard's wars, the dying king forgives him outright: live on, he says, and by my bounty see the light of day.
stops.quote: Live on, and by my bounty behold the light of day.
stops.quote_source: attributed last mercy of Richard I to his killer, Châlus-Chabrol, March 1199 (tradition, Roger of Howden)
suggested_refs: The ruined keep of Châlus-Chabrol, above the Tardoire in the Limousin, where Richard received his death wound
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Ralph of Coggeshall, Chronicon Anglicanum

stops.name: Fontevraud and Rouen, the burial divided
stops.campa: Richard dies on the sixth of April in his mother's arms; Mercadier, his mercenary captain, flays the boy who killed him alive despite the pardon, a mercy his own men refuse to honor. His body, by his own instruction, is divided in the old royal fashion: heart embalmed and sent to Rouen, to lie in its own small tomb in the cathedral; entrails left near Châlus, by one tradition at the abbey of Charroux; the rest carried to Fontevraud in Anjou and laid beside the father he fought nearly all his life, under an effigy holding a crown he wore, in the end, for barely six months at home.
suggested_refs: The painted effigy tombs of Henry II, Eleanor of Aquitaine, and Richard I at Fontevraud Abbey; the separate heart-tomb at Rouen Cathedral
sources: Roger of Howden, Gesta Regis Ricardi
Ralph of Coggeshall, Chronicon Anglicanum
analysis of the embalmed heart of Richard I, Scientific Reports (2013)
